title: Applications in Descope
Who calls whom, and why it matters

slides.title: One question sorts every app: who is calling whom?

pillars.title: Inbound: Third-Party
pillars.text: Someone else's app calls YOUR API on behalf of one of your users. The user (or their admin) approves exactly what is shared. Think: "Zapier wants to read your HubSpot contacts. Allow?"

pillars.title: Inbound: M2M
pillars.text: Someone else's server calls YOUR API with no person in the loop. It proves who it is with a client ID and secret and gets a scoped token. Think: a nightly sync job.

pillars.title: Outbound
pillars.text: YOUR app calls someone else's API (Google, Slack, Salesforce) on behalf of your user. Descope connects the account, stores the token, and keeps it fresh.

slides.title: The three apps at a glance
Inbound Third-Party: a valet key for your API
slides.intro: You do not hand the valet your house keys, just a key that starts the car. Third-party access works the same way.

cards.title: What it is
bullets: Your product becomes the place partners "connect to"
A partner app gets limited, revocable access to a user's data
No passwords are ever shared with the partner

cards.title: How it works
bullets: Partner sends the user to your Descope /authorize page
User signs in and sees a consent screen with the scopes
Descope issues tokens; the partner calls your API with them

cards.title: What Descope handles
bullets: OAuth 2.0 / OIDC authorization server endpoints
Consent screens built in Flows, your branding
Policy sets the max scopes; users can approve less
Revoke a partner app at any time

slides.title: You have used this a hundred times
slides.intro: Every "Connect your account" button on a partner site is an inbound third-party app, seen from the side that owns the data.

cards.title: Zapier -> HubSpot
bullets: You build a Zap: new HubSpot contact -> Slack message
Zapier sends you to HubSpot to log in
HubSpot shows: "Zapier wants to read contacts"
HubSpot owns the API, so for HubSpot, Zapier is an inbound third-party app

cards.title: Calendly -> Google Calendar
bullets: Calendly needs to see when you are busy
Google shows a consent screen listing calendar access
Remove it later in your Google account settings
For Google, Calendly is an inbound third-party app

cards.title: Installing an app in Slack
bullets: A workspace admin adds Asana to Slack
The admin approves the scopes once for the whole workspace
Every member can use it without re-consenting
Tenant-level consent, the B2B version of the same idea

pillars.title: Partner asks
pillars.text: The user clicks "Connect" in the partner app. The partner redirects to your Descope /authorize URL with the scopes it wants.

pillars.title: User decides
pillars.text: The user signs in with your normal login flow and sees what is being requested. They approve all, some, or none.

pillars.title: Descope issues tokens
pillars.text: The partner exchanges a one-time code for an access token and refresh token, limited to the approved scopes.

pillars.title: Your API enforces
pillars.text: Your API validates the token and checks scopes on every call. Revoke the app and access stops immediately.

slides.title: Inbound M2M: a badge for a server
slides.intro: No browser, no login screen, no person. A backend service proves who it is and gets exactly the access it needs.

cards.title: What it is
bullets: A trusted server or job calls your API directly
Used for syncs, batch jobs, integrations, and backend partners
Access is defined up front, not consented per user

cards.title: How it works
bullets: Descope gives the client a client ID and client secret
The server calls /token with grant_type=client_credentials
It gets a short-lived access token and calls your API

cards.title: What Descope handles
bullets: Issues and rotates client credentials
Policies decide which scopes each client gets
Short-lived tokens, so a leaked token expires fast
Import existing client credentials when migrating

slides.title: M2M in the real world
slides.intro: If a developer pasted a client ID and secret into a server config, that is machine-to-machine.

cards.title: PayPal REST API
bullets: Merchants create an app and get a client ID + secret
Their server trades them for an OAuth access token
No shopper ever logs in to get that token
Classic client credentials

cards.title: Spotify Web API
bullets: An app wants public catalog data: albums, artists, tracks
It uses the client credentials flow, app identity only
No user, so no access to anyone's playlists
Shows how scopes stay narrow without a user

cards.title: Your B2B customer's backend
bullets: A customer's ERP pushes orders into your API every night
You give them a Descope M2M client per tenant
Their job fetches a token, then calls your API
Rotate or revoke one customer without touching others

slides.title: Third-Party vs M2M: same door, different visitor

options.title: Inbound: Third-Party
options.subtitle: Acts on behalf of a user
bullets: Authorization code flow, PKCE for SPAs and mobile
Token carries the user's identity
Use when the partner needs a specific user's data

options.title: Inbound: M2M
options.subtitle: Acts as itself
bullets: Client credentials flow
Token carries the client's identity
Use for syncs, jobs, and server-to-server integrations

slides.title: Outbound: your app reaches out to other services
slides.intro: Inbound is others calling you. Outbound is you calling Google, Slack, Salesforce, or HubSpot for your user.

cards.title: What it is
bullets: Your user connects their account at another provider
Your app then calls that provider's API on their behalf
A token vault, so you never build OAuth plumbing per provider

cards.title: How it works
bullets: User clicks "Connect Google" in your app (Flow or SDK)
They consent on Google's own screen
Descope stores the tokens; your backend fetches them when needed

cards.title: What Descope handles
bullets: Prebuilt providers: Google, Slack, Salesforce, HubSpot and more
Secure token storage per user or per tenant
Automatic refresh before tokens expire
Progressive scopes: ask for more only when needed

slides.title: Outbound in the real world
slides.intro: Every product with an "Integrations" or "Connected accounts" page is managing outbound tokens.

cards.title: Calendly
bullets: Connects to your Google or Outlook calendar
Reads busy times, writes new meetings
Has to keep the token alive for months
Without a vault: custom OAuth code per calendar provider

cards.title: HubSpot
bullets: Connects a rep's Gmail or Outlook inbox
Logs sent emails to the CRM automatically
Thousands of reps, one token each
Refresh failures mean silent data gaps

cards.title: Canva
bullets: Import images from Google Drive or Dropbox
Ask for file access only when the user clicks import
That is progressive scoping in practice
Start small, request more at the moment of need

pillars.title: The handshake
pillars.text: A Calendly user clicks "Connect Google Calendar", signs in at Google, and approves calendar access.

pillars.title: Google's view: Inbound Third-Party
pillars.text: Google owns the data. Calendly is a third-party app it issued scoped, revocable tokens to.

pillars.title: Calendly's view: Outbound
pillars.text: Calendly calls someone else's API. It must store Google's tokens and refresh them. That is an Outbound App.

slides.title: Expose it to your users: drop-in web components
slides.intro: Descope widgets are embeddable web components: add the UI in a few lines instead of building it.

cards.title: Outbound Applications widget
bullets: A "Connected accounts" page inside your product
Users connect or disconnect Google, Slack, Salesforce
Think of Calendly's calendar connections screen
Tokens land in the Descope vault automatically

cards.title: Applications Portal widget
bullets: A user-facing list of the apps they can open
One place for users to launch connected apps
Embed in your app or host it in the Admin Portal

cards.title: Access Key widgets
bullets: B2B admins create and rotate their own API keys
Users can manage personal keys for scripts and jobs
Self-service M2M setup, no support tickets
Scoped to the customer's tenant

slides.title: Which app do I need?
rows: Let partners build "Connect to <your product>" integrations
Let a B2B customer's admin approve an integration for their whole org
Let a partner's server or nightly job call your API
Read a user's Google Calendar, Slack, or CRM data from your app
Do both: partners call you, and you call Google for the same user

slides.title: Let others in. Reach out safely.
slides.subtitle: Descope handles OAuth on both sides, so your team ships integrations, not plumbing.
